Unemployment rate rises to 4.9 per cent
The unemployment rate rose to 4.9% in October, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
This is the highest unemployment rate since October 2021, the ABS said.

Youth unemployment surges
Here's what the ABS has had to say about the jump in Australia's unemployment rate:
The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose to 4.9 per cent in October, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
This is the highest unemployment rate since October 2021.
''In October, there were 44,000 less employed people and 18,000 more unemployed people." ABS head of labour statistics, Sean Crick, said.
''Similar to last month, we had a higher proportion of people remaining unemployed than we would usually see in October in the post-Covid era.

''The youth unemployment rate – that is, for people aged between 15 and 24 – increased to 11.3% in October from 11.1% in September. This is the highest it’s been since October 2021. In the post-Covid period (from May 2022 onwards), the youth unemployment rate has averaged 9.2%."
RBA rate hike bets may change substantially
New ABS data showing the unemployment rate jumping to 4.9 per cent will reduce bets of an RBA interest rate hike in December.
Depending on the trend in employment, it may rule out another interest rate hike for this cycle.
Stay tuned for expert reactions from economists across the country.
Dollar falls under 67 US cents
The Australian dollar has fallen to a new 10-month low of 66.9 US cents following the release of the latest unemployment data.
Unemployment rate jumps to 4.9 per cent
The unemployment rate for October has risen sharply to 4.9%, from 4.7% in September, seasonally adjusted.
Roughly 43,500 jobs were shed in the month while the participation rate fell by 0.2%.
The Reserve Bank has stated that an unemployment rate between 4.5% and 5% would be needed to bring inflation back down to its target range of between 2 and 3%.

Administrators appointed to General Pants Co confirm business as usual
Jason Tracy and Glen Kanevsky of Alvarez & Marsal have been appointed Voluntary Administrators of the clothing retailer General Pants.
The appointment took place last night and includes nine related entities.
They confirmed that all 35 General Pants stores across Australia and NZ, as well as its online store, remain open and trading as usual.

The Administrators have taken control of the business and are working closely with the existing management team to urgently assess the business, including its trading performance, stores, stock and costs.

"General Pants Co is one of Australia's best-known youth fashion brands, with a loyal customer base and a dedicated team. Our immediate priorities are to keep the stores trading, support employees and customers, and pursue a sale and/or recapitalisation of the business," says Joint Administrator Jason Tracy.
"With Black Friday next week, we are focused on maximising trading performance and expect strong demand over the period.
"We thank the team members, landlords and suppliers of General Pants Co for their support as we work through the administration."
The business employs about 500 people across Australia and New Zealand, with administrators confirming employees will continue to be paid for the work they do during the administration.
Employee entitlements accrued prior to the appointment remain protected under the Corporations Act, with employee entitlements ranking ahead of most other unsecured creditor claims.
The first creditors meeting will be held by Monday 30 November 2026, within eight business days of the appointment.
Creditors will receive written notice of the meeting.

Key Event
Worst migrant underpayment is least likely to face scrutiny, says report
A new study of migrant working conditions in Australia has exposed large-scale impunity for exploitation throughout Australia.
The Migrant Justice Institute (MJI) study, the largest of its kind to date, found that employers responsible for the worst cases of wage theft are the least likely to face consequences.
Researchers analysed almost 10,000 migrant responses from those who worked on a temporary visa, including international students, sponsored workers and backpackers.
Six out of seven underpaid migrants never tried to get the wages they were owed.
The report found a fear of losing their job or visa keeps the overwhelming majority silent, with many viewing legal processes as too complex and unlikely to deliver results.

"For international students and other migrants, underpayment is now the expected price of a job in Australia," says co-author Bassina Farbenblum, Associate Professor of UNSW Law & Justice and Co-Executive Director of MJI."When your employer controls next week’s shifts and speaking up could jeopardise your job and your visa, putting up with wage theft in silence is often the rational choice."

"For international students and other migrants, underpayment is now the expected price of a job in Australia," says co-author Bassina Farbenblum, Associate Professor of UNSW Law & Justice and Co-Executive Director of MJI.
"When your employer controls next week’s shifts and speaking up could jeopardise your job and your visa, putting up with wage theft in silence is often the rational choice."

Co-author Laurie Berg, Associate Professor of University of Technology Sydney Law and Co-Executive Director of MJI says "government enforcement has been limited", meaning "dishonest employers have no realistic expectation of getting caught".
"Wage theft from migrants remains cost-free for the businesses that profit from it across many industries."
Migrants who were underpaid the most per hour were least likely to take action.
Despite three in five underpaid migrant workers knowing about the Fair Work Ombudsman, only 3% approached the regulator.
After two years of operation, only one business was listed on the Prohibited Employer Register.

"Government enforcement must be substantially ramped up. The Fair Work Ombudsman needs to enforce the law at scale where dishonest employers expect to be caught. Wage recovery processes must be accessible and reliably deliver results," says Berg.

"Government must urgently create a system that makes it safe and worthwhile for migrants to speak up. The research has sounded the alarm on widespread exploitation of international students. It’s critical that universities and government now partner to get students the help and protections they need," says Farbenblum.

Transparent auction pricing seems to be working, according to data
On the topic of housing, new laws in Victoria that require home sellers to publish the price they want to sell at appear to be working.
The laws aim to reduce underquoting and help buyers know what a property will sell for by requiring a disclosed "reserve" price.
Property platform Homer has compiled the data for the first month since the practice became law in Victoria, for sales from October 16.
"The data does suggest transparency is working," Homer chief executive Henry Pedersen says.
He says properties that sold at auction went for a median of 0.9% above the published reserve price.
"So buyers and sellers are landing very close to what was advertised," he says.

Sydney to lead Australia's housing price recovery, analysis predicts
Australia's housing market downturn is set to drag on in every major city into next year, but new analysis suggests Sydney will bounce back and lead a national price recovery.
Domain's forecast predicts house prices will fall between 10 and 13 per cent across major capital cities by mid-2027, driven by high borrowing costs and weak buyer confidence.
In Sydney, house prices are expected to drop by 10 per cent by June 2027 before stabilising in the second half of the year.
According to the forecast, median prices are expected to increase from $1.6 million to $1.7 million over the 12 months to December 2027.

What could the Anthropic IPO mean for shareholders?
A high valuation for Anthropic could increase value for large shareholders like Amazon and Alphabet (parent company of Google), which own around a third of the company.
Another existing investor is Zoom Communications, which invested in 2023.
At the time, the amount was not disclosed, but a later Zoom filing showed $US51 million in "strategic investments".
The investment was part of a partnership announced at the time, under which Zoom would use the Claude AI assistant.

"Collaborating with Zoom allows us to bring robust, steerable AI to more people in the workplace," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said at the time."We are excited to showcase Anthropic's and Zoom's commitment to boosting productivity through AI-enabled solutions that prioritise safety and helpfulness."

Nvidia shares drop 3 per cent
Despite yesterday's strong earnings results from tech giant Nvidia, shares have dipped about -3% as Wall Street closes for Wednesday afternoon.

Since its October 6 record high, Nvidia shares have fallen 36%, with much of that drop related to the company's co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, which came after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two with Nvidia employees.

Following Nvidia's strong report and outlook, the average analyst estimate for its adjusted net income in its next fiscal year has climbed to $US393 billion from $US380 billion, according to LSEG data.
At the same time, the average analyst price target has dipped to $US251.74 from $US265.70 on Monday.

Higher earnings estimates and lower price targets suggest analysts believe Nvidia’s business remains strong but are applying a more cautious valuation, reflecting risks around the CEO transition and AI spending.
Nvidia shares closed at $US151 per share.

Anthropic prepares for one of the largest IPO's in history
Anthropic is preparing for one of the largest initial public offerings in history.
The offering could raise up to $US64.4 billion and put it at a valuation exceeding $US1 trillion.

The US company behind the artificial intelligence assistant Claude plans to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday (US time), with an estimated offering price between $US70 and $US78 per share.
According to Reuters, it anticipates selling 825 million shares and an additional private placement of $US26 billion among strategic investors.
Founded in 2021 by specialists who previously worked at OpenAI, including Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic competes with ChatGPT and Gemini through Claude.
Its growth has focused on providing tools to companies for analysing information, developing software programs, and automating activities.
It also generates revenue from companies that integrate Claude into their products and operations.
